General Strike Brings Business Activity to Standstill Across Bosnia and Herzegovina

A nationwide general strike has brought economic activity across Bosnia and Herzegovina to a virtual halt, as public and private sector workers downed tools on Thursday in protest over stagnant wages, rising living costs, and stalled labor reforms. The strike, organized by a coalition of trade unions representing transport, healthcare, education, and manufacturing employees, is the most widespread industrial action in the country in more than two decades.

Major transport hubs in Sarajevo, Banja Luka, and Mostar reported near-total shutdowns, with local bus and rail services suspended and freight traffic at the Port of Ploče experiencing significant delays. The Federation of BiH Chamber of Commerce estimated that as many as 60% of factories operated by companies such as MetalPro Engineering and AgroBalkan Foods halted production lines as workers joined picket lines.

Healthcare services were reduced to emergency-only care, frustrating patients and prompting the Ministry of Health to issue an appeal for dialogue. Schools across the country closed their doors, leaving parents scrambling for childcare. Government offices were shuttered, delaying the processing of business permits and tax filings.

Union leaders say the strike comes after months of failed negotiations with state and entity-level authorities. "Our members are struggling to make ends meet while inflation erodes their paychecks," said Adnan Kovačević, president of the United Workers' Federation. "We are demanding a 15% wage increase and urgent reforms to the labor code."

Economic analysts warn that a prolonged shutdown could dampen Bosnia and Herzegovina's modest growth prospects for 2024. "Every day of lost output is a blow to an already fragile recovery," said Ivana Marković, senior economist at Balkan Insight Analytics.

The Ministry of Finance declined to provide an estimate of the economic impact but urged all parties to return to the negotiating table. In a brief statement, it acknowledged "the legitimate concerns of workers" but called for "restraint and constructive engagement."

At the time of writing, union representatives and government officials remained deadlocked, with no breakthrough in sight. The general strike is expected to continue into Friday, with further disruptions anticipated.
